## Project summary

### Project title and location

The proposed project, **Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan**, will support the fictional coastal city of Harbor Point to reduce exposure to extreme heat and street flooding between 2027 and 2032. The plan was adopted by the Harbor Point City Council on 14 March 2026 and serves a city with 182,400 residents.

[Information needed: Confirm the country in which Harbor Point is located for the GCF SAP proposal.]

### Delivery arrangements

The Office of Climate Resilience will lead delivery in partnership with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works will deliver green stormwater infrastructure; the Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions; and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents.

The Coastal Resilience Finance Corporation is the GCF-accredited entity that will submit and oversee the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.

### Scope, duration and financing

The project will deliver 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors in Eastside and Millbrook, 85 bioretention cells, 3.2 hectares of permeable green schoolyard play areas, and 18 community cooling centres.

The total programme cost is USD 26.5 million. Harbor Point will contribute USD 7.9 million from its capital budget, while USD 18.6 million is sought in external grant funding. The planned implementation period is 2027–2032.

[Information needed: Confirm the amount of GCF grant funding requested for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan and whether it comprises the full USD 18.6 million external grant requirement.]

The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres, with extended opening hours on days above 32 °C.

The Coastal Resilience Finance Corporation is the GCF-accredited entity that will submit, oversee and provide fiduciary management for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan SAP proposal.

The Harbor Point City Council adopted the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan on 14 March 2026. The Office of Climate Resilience and the Department of Public Works will lead project delivery, with delivery roles for the Harbor Point Unified School District and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance as described above.

### Monitoring, reporting and learning

edited_chapters.climate_context:
## Climate rationale and baseline

Harbor Point faces compound climate-related risks from extreme heat and stormwater flooding. The proposed Harbor Point Cool and Dry Streets Programme addresses these risks between 2027 and 2032 through urban greening, green stormwater infrastructure and community cooling measures.

### Extreme heat

Harbor Point recorded 23 days above 35 °C in 2025, compared with an average of 9 such days per year during 1991–2020. Heat-related emergency department visits increased from 140 in 2021 to 310 in 2025.

Eastside and Millbrook have the city’s lowest tree-canopy cover, at 11 percent and 13 percent respectively.

### Stormwater flooding

Street flooding affects 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event. The Canal Street underpass closed six times in 2025 because of standing water. In Eastside, the existing drainage network was designed for a 5-year storm and is undersized for current rainfall intensities.

### Exposed population and assets

Harbor Point has 182,400 residents. The cool corridors are planned in Eastside and Millbrook, which have the lowest tree canopy in the city, and Eastside’s drainage network is undersized for current rainfall intensities. Documented flood exposure includes 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event and the Canal Street underpass.

[Information needed: Confirm the number and characteristics of people exposed to extreme heat and stormwater flooding in Eastside and Millbrook, including any priority groups to be targeted by the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Baseline conditions and need for intervention

The project responds to documented heat and flooding conditions through an integrated package of measures. The baseline includes low tree-canopy cover in Eastside and Millbrook, recurring heat-related emergency department visits, flood-prone intersections, and drainage infrastructure that is inadequate for current rainfall intensities. These conditions provide the rationale for increasing shade and canopy, improving local rainwater capture, and making cooling facilities available during days above 32 °C.
edited_chapters.project_components:
## Project components and activities

The Harbor Point Cool and Dry Streets Programme will implement an integrated package of urban greening, green stormwater infrastructure and community cooling measures between 2027 and 2032.

### Component 1: Cool corridors

The project will plant 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors connecting schools, clinics and transit stops in Eastside and Millbrook. Activities will include tree planting and three years of establishment watering. The intended outcome is to increase tree canopy cover in both neighbourhoods to 25 percent by 2032.

Cool-corridor planting and establishment watering are estimated to cost USD 9.6 million.

### Component 2: Green stormwater infrastructure

The project will construct 85 bioretention cells and convert 3.2 hectares of asphalt schoolyards into permeable green play areas. Together, these measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface.

Green stormwater infrastructure activities will include design and construction supervision and are estimated to cost USD 14.2 million.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 85 bioretention cells and the schoolyards to be converted into 3.2 hectares of permeable green play areas under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Component 3: Community cooling network

The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres. These centres will have extended opening hours on days above 32 °C to provide accessible cooling facilities during extreme-heat conditions.

The community cooling network is estimated to cost USD 2.7 million and is funded from the city operating budget.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 18 libraries and recreation centres to be designated as community cooling centres under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Delivery roles

The Office of Climate Resilience will lead delivery together with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works will deliver the green stormwater infrastructure component; the Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions; and Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents.

### Expected adaptation results

The Harbor Point Cool and Dry Streets Programme is intended to reduce exposure to extreme heat and street flooding between 2027 and 2032. Expected results include increased shade and urban tree canopy along routes connecting schools, clinics and transit stops; improved local capture of rainfall from impervious surfaces; and accessible cooling facilities during days above 32 °C.

The project will deliver 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors, 85 bioretention cells, 3.2 hectares of permeable green schoolyard play areas, and 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres. The green stormwater measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface.

### Beneficiaries

The cool corridors serve Eastside and Millbrook, where tree-canopy cover is currently 11 percent and 13 percent respectively, and where Eastside’s drainage network is undersized for current rainfall intensities. The cool corridors connect schools, clinics and transit stops, and the 18 community cooling centres are located in libraries and recreation centres.
